newsitem.title: FRANCE: Trichet defends French monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: Trichet defends French monetary policy.

text.p: Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet on Thursday strongly defended the country's strong monetary policy, saying it resulted in France having the third-lowest interest rates in the world.

Appearing on French television LCI, Trichet refused to comment directly on calls by former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing and two Bank of France council members for a weaker currency to boost the sluggish economy.

But thanks to France's decade-old policy of keeping the franc steady against the mark, it now enjoyed the third lowest interest rates in the world, after Japan and Switzerland, due to the confidence of investors, who were not necessarily "devoted francophiles," he said.
"When one has a stable currency, it's good for growth and good for jobs because it preserves competitiveness of companies," he said.
The policy was clearly not penalising France in terms of exports, as the country boasted the third-biggest trade surplus in the world.
And he said a large majority of the French are attached to having a currency that holds its value.
Trichet reiterated that the ailing economy was looking up and urged the French to have confidence in the future.

"We have real prospects of a rebound in European economic growth," he said. "We have no right to be so lacking in confidence." He said that, according to various economic institutes, the French economy had "passed the trough," echoing comments he made in London on Wednesday that stronger growth was clearly under way in France and the rest of Europe.
While France was a prosperous country, it did have difficulty translating its wealth into job creation, he said, citing record 12.6 percent unemployment.
But France was not alone among European countries in having such a problem, he said, pointing to neighbouring Belgium and other countries whose unemployment is also high.
While structural changes were needed to lower French unemployment, he did not believe France could import job creation solutions that went against its social values.
France could look to the Netherlands for some ideas.

"They have around seven percent unemployment. We have 12.6 percent. If we had the same amount of part-time work in the competitive private sector that exists in the Netherlands, there would be one million fewer unemployed in France," he said.
